stories.title: Elorian's first AI model, Glimpse, targets image and video reasoning
stories.summary: Startup Elorian launched its first AI model, Glimpse, built to reason with images rather than just about them, which it says beats GPT-6 Astra on scientific chart reasoning and video captioning.
stories.more: According to Elorian's own evaluations, Glimpse outperforms GPT-6 Astra on scientific chart reasoning and short-form video captioning tasks. The company also reports competitive results on other visual reasoning benchmarks. No independent verification of these results was mentioned.

items.title: Elorian’s first AI model wants to reason with images, not just about them
items.excerpt: According to Elorian's evaluations, Glimpse outperforms even GPT-6 Astra on scientific chart reasoning and short-form video captioning, with competitive results on other visual reasoning tasks.

stories.title: Google's Gemini 4 Argon nears the AI frontier on ARC-AGI-3
stories.summary: Google DeepMind's Gemini 4 Argon scored 97.5% on the ARC-AGI-3 benchmark, making Google the second lab after OpenAI to pass 95%, though it still trails rivals on math and coding.
stories.more: The 97.5 percent score was achieved outside the benchmark's standard test harness; under standard conditions, Argon's score drops to 49.8 percent, showing results swing wildly depending on setup. Argon also still trails rival models in math and software engineering benchmarks. Google is now the second AI lab, after OpenAI, to cross the 95 percent mark on ARC-AGI-3 in any configuration.

items.title: Google's Gemini 4 Argon is closer to the AI frontier than any Google model in months
items.excerpt: Google Deepmind's Gemini 4 Argon scored 97.5 percent on the ARC-AGI-3 benchmark, making Google the second lab after OpenAI to cross the 95 percent mark. But the results swing wildly depending on the test setup: in the standard harness, the score drops to just 49.8 percent. Argon also trails rivals in math and software engineering. stories.title: Veritas expands anti-counterfeit verification chip to jewelry and fragrance
stories.summary: Startup Veritas is expanding its chip-based anti-counterfeit verification technology to jewelry, trophies, and fragrance bottles, aiming to catch so-called 'superfakes.'
stories.more: Veritas builds a physical chip that verifies the authenticity of luxury goods, targeting counterfeiters who have gotten better at replicating brand marks closely enough to pass as genuine ('superfakes'). The expansion extends the chip's use beyond its initial product categories into jewelry, trophies, and fragrance bottles.

items.excerpt: Counterfeiters are getting better at replicating brands' marks and passing off dupes, known as "superfakes," as genuine items. A startup called Veritas wants to tackle the problem with its own chip that verifies goods.

stories.more: The plan is currently limited to research labs based at US universities that don't already have an enterprise contract with OpenAI. It offers up to 30 free seats, each valid for one year. No further detail on which OpenAI products or tiers are included was given in the excerpt.

stories.title: Meta's new terms may let it train AI on news publishers' sites for free
stories.summary: Meta's updated business terms, taking effect October 30th, appear to let it crawl and scrape content from sites 'associated' with businesses on its platforms, including news publishers, to train AI.
stories.more: The new terms were first reported by Nieman Lab and apply to websites 'associated' with businesses that use Meta's platforms, including online publishers. Meta says it can use this outside content to 'develop, improve, research,' and 'train' its AI systems. Legal experts cited by Ars Technica describe the streamlined commercial terms of service as a way for Meta to avoid millions of dollars in AI licensing fees it might otherwise owe publishers. The terms take effect October 30th.

stories.title: MIT's Sherry Turkle argues chatbots shouldn't speak as 'I' or 'me'
stories.summary: MIT professor Sherry Turkle warns that people are becoming dangerously enmeshed with chatbots, and argues AI systems shouldn't be allowed to refer to themselves as 'I' or 'me.'
stories.more: Turkle's concern centers on how first-person language from chatbots can deepen users' emotional attachment to them. The piece frames this as part of a broader worry about people's growing reliance on and attachment to conversational AI. No specific policy or product proposal was described beyond the framing of the concern.

stories.title: New essay claims AI interpretability may be closer than researchers thought
stories.summary: A new essay argues neural networks may be far easier to interpret than assumed, with about 90% of neurons serving a clear function — a claim researchers are still debating.
stories.more: If the thesis holds, it would be significant for AI safety research, since deceptive or dangerous behavior could potentially be spotted directly in a model's internal circuits. The essay's claim that roughly 90 percent of neurons have a clear, identifiable function has split the research community, with researchers still debating whether it holds up.

stories.title: New FDE-Gym benchmark tests AI agents on messy real-world delivery work
stories.summary: FDE-Gym is a new benchmark of 95 end-to-end delivery tasks from 20 customer scenarios across 18 sectors, testing AI agents on ambiguous, live-system work instead of well-specified tickets.
stories.more: The benchmark was adapted by industry experts from real-world delivery projects rather than synthetic tasks. It targets the gap between typical agent benchmarks, which use well-specified issue reports or tickets, and real customer delivery, where forward-deployed engineers must clarify ambiguous requirements, work in live systems, and uncover unstated constraints. The 95 tasks are drawn from 20 customer scenarios spanning 18 industry sectors.

stories.title: Ex-Nvidia robotics marketer says the field hasn't had its ChatGPT moment
stories.summary: Amulya Vishwanath, who led product marketing for Nvidia's robotics platforms for seven years and now invests in the field, says robotics is still in its 'Lego era.'
stories.more: Vishwanath argues that fundamentals like actuators, robotic hands, software, and safety standards are still being rebuilt from scratch. That puts her view at odds with others in the industry who believe a general foundation model could soon give robotics its own 'ChatGPT moment.' TechCrunch published her comments as both a video interview and a podcast episode.

stories.title: Mark Wahlberg says he's open to AI using his likeness after he's gone
stories.summary: Actor and angel investor Mark Wahlberg says he's comfortable with AI being used in filmmaking 'the right way,' and is open to an AI clone continuing his legacy.
stories.more: Wahlberg said he's fine with AI in film as long as it's used to 'enhance what you're doing' rather than replace creative work outright. He also said he'd be open to an AI clone of himself carrying on his legacy after he's gone. Wahlberg is also an active angel investor, per TechCrunch.
